👩‍🎓 About me

Civil engineering student with an eye for the site

I am a 7th-semester Civil Engineering student at KLE Technological University. I have keen observation skills on construction sites: I notice how a site is organised, how materials, labour and vehicles move through it, and where limited space or missing paperwork starts to cause problems.

This portfolio shows that approach in practice. I visited two live sites, studied the approvals a project needs, and turned what I saw into a site layout, a concrete cost study and working systems for stores, surveying, wastage and labour.

Solutions

What I saw on site

Two site visits in Hubballi showed me how real teams handle space, storage and paperwork.

Rokhade Castle, Vidyanagar

  • Vertical mixed-use building, 7,200 sq ft, 1st floor centering under way (20 Aug 2026)
  • One access point leading to the basement; no separate pedestrian and vehicle roads
  • Materials stored about 10 m away and labour housed at a distance because space was short
  • The site engineer did not know the RERA and permission documents

Shriya Serenity, Gokul Road

  • Commercial building, 75,000 sq ft, RERA approved (21 Aug 2026)
  • Large open yard allowed organised storage and clearer circulation
  • Shows how an approved project keeps its paperwork and site organisation in order

Interaction with site engineers

  • Raju Hiremath, site engineer at Rokhade Castle: he did not know the RERA and permission documents, so I studied the full set from the RERA and local-body requirements.
  • Veeresh Byahatti at Shriya Serenity: the site is RERA approved, and I used it to see how an approved project is organised.

Labour housing and storage rules

Under the BOCW Act, 1996 (Sections 32 to 34) and the Karnataka BOCW Rules, 2006, the employer must give free, safe accommodation at or near the site. I sized the camp from the Karnataka Labour Department board.

Phased site layout

The site is built in three phases so the working zone moves while stores, office and labour camp stay safe behind a temporary barricade. Tap a phase to see it.

Layout decisions

  • Heavy vehicles and material logistics use their own gate; staff, visitors and labour use the other, so trucks and people do not cross.
  • Staging, storage, site office and testing lab sit inside completed blocks, close to the working zone and to each other.
  • Labour accommodation stays at the far end, away from the crane and concrete zone.
  • CP marks the gate check posts where every entry is logged.

Concrete conveying

  • Transit mixers carry concrete from the plant to each block, and a concrete pump with placing boom serves the basement and upper floors.
  • The plant sits near the heavy-vehicle gate so every block is reached without crossing the labour zone.
  • Cement silo, sand and aggregate bunkers stand beside the plant for short loader runs.

Yards, lab and utilities

  • Carpenter and fabricator yards sit beside the staging area, with covered storage for plywood, bars and cutting machines.
  • Material testing lab and store stand next to each other so samples reach the lab quickly.
  • Power: temporary panel boards, earthing and a DG set for backup. Water: storage tanks for curing, mixing and the labour camp, sized from the headcount.

Reflection

Two real sites taught me that a layout is decided by space and paperwork before drawings. One site kept materials and labour away from the building because it was cramped, and its engineer did not know the RERA documents; the RERA-approved site was clearly better organised. Pricing a plant against RMC showed me that the saving exists only because 12,000 m³ over 18 months spreads the fixed cost.

Conclusion

A three-phase layout with separate gates for vehicles and people, complete RERA and local-body paperwork, a BOCW-compliant labour camp and our own batching plant (₹4,870 against ₹5,080 per m³, saving about ₹25.15 lakh) gives an efficient, compliant site for the 468-day programme.

📦 Problem statement 2

Procurement, quality check and store system

A new store manager should be able to run the store from a fixed routine, with the project manager checking only the records.

Problem statement 2

(Theme: To develop a system for construction material procurement, QC, storage and accounts which can be sustainable with minimum supervision from the project manager)

As the project manager for this project, you just hired a new store manager but he lacks the experience required to handle large scale projects. The project starts in 15 days from today. For the efficient movement of materials in and out of the construction site, you are supposed to set up a material procurement system which can sustain with your minimum involvement once the project starts. The following conditions must be met through your system.

  • Prepare the layout of the store keeping in mind the consumables, non-consumables, equipment, and safety gear.
  • The construction site has 2 gates, based on the location of the store in the site, decide which gate will be used as ingress and for departure.
  • All vehicles numbers must be recorded when they enter and exit the site. You are free to use security and technology available at your disposal to accomplish this.
  • The materials vehicle driver must bring in the invoice. A copy must remain at the security, one with the store manager and one copy must go to the accounts section.
  • The materials must pass certain quality checks, please ensure the QA/QC inspector is working with the store manager for the inspection of the materials. Keep in mind the proximity of the material testing lab with the store. If rejected, the material must leave the premises immediately. Proper paperwork must be maintained.
  • Accepted material after quality check must go to their designated storage slot as defined during Site Layout planning.

Minutes of meeting

Tuesday 18/08/2026 · in class

Work distribution for Problem 2.

TaskMember
Gate entry and exit register for every vehicleAnirudh
Store layout: consumables, non-consumables, equipment and safety gearGayathri
Three-copy invoice flow: security, store manager, accountsMaitrey
QA/QC inspection with the store manager, lab proximity and rejected-material procedureNandish

Solutions

Site visited and interaction with engineer

  • Sites visited: Rokhade Castle (Vidyanagar) and Shriya Serenity (Gokul Road).
  • At Rokhade Castle, cement was kept in covered godowns and aggregates in heaps, and materials were stored about 10 m from the site because space was short. This is why the store sits next to the gate and the lab in my plan.
  • Engineer interaction: see Problem 1.
  1. Gate in. Material trucks enter by the heavy-vehicle gate. Security logs vehicle number, driver, time and material, using ANPR or a simple register.
  2. Three invoice copies. One stays with security, one goes to the store manager, one goes to accounts.
  3. Inspection. The QA/QC inspector and store manager check quantity, brand, batch and test certificates, with samples sent to the lab next to the store.
  4. Accept or reject. Rejected loads get a rejection note and leave at once through the same gate. Accepted material is tagged and moved to its marked slot.
  5. Record. Goods received note, stock ledger and issue slip are updated the same day; accounts pay only against all three matching.

Store layout

  • Cement godown: raised floor, dry, stacked 10 bags high at most
  • Steel yard on racks by diameter, sand and aggregate in bunkers
  • Consumables, non-consumables, equipment and safety gear in separate zones
  • Flammables and gas cylinders away from the rest, as the Karnataka board shows

Gate rule

  • Entry through the heavy-vehicle gate near the store, one-way loop inside
  • Labour and staff use the other gate, so people never walk through the unloading zone
  • Weekly stock check by the project manager against the ledger

Detailed solution

Step-by-step procedure for the new store manager

  1. Indent and order. The site engineer raises an indent from the weekly plan. The project manager approves it before a purchase order goes to the vendor.
  2. Vendor selection. Compare at least three quotes on rate, quality certificates, delivery time and credit terms, then keep an approved vendor list.
  3. Receiving. Security logs the truck, the store manager checks the challan against the purchase order, and QA/QC inspects the material.
  4. Accept or reject. Accepted material gets a goods received note and a tag. Rejected material gets a rejection note signed by the driver and leaves at once.
  5. Payment. Accounts pays only when the purchase order, goods received note and invoice match (three-way match).
  6. Issue. Material leaves the store only against a signed issue slip, and the ledger balance is updated the same day.

Quality checks on arrival

MaterialWhat the inspector checks
CementBrand, grade, manufacture date, intact bags, no lumps, bag weight on a sample
SteelGrade and size, mill test certificate, rust, weight check against the standard
Sand and aggregateGrading, silt and dust, moisture, size against the order
Plywood and formworkThickness, surface condition, count
Safety gearCertification, size, issue register

Store rules

  • First in, first out for cement, with bags stacked on a raised platform and away from walls.
  • Reorder level fixed for each item so stock never runs out.
  • Monthly physical stock count signed by the store manager and the engineer.

Records to keep

  • Vehicle register, challan file, goods received notes, issue slips and rejection notes.
  • Daily stock sheet and weekly report to the project manager.
  • Invoice copies filed three ways: security, store, accounts.

Reflection

The main lesson of this problem is that a store should not depend on one clever person. If the routine is written down and every step leaves a record, a new store manager can pick it up on day one.

  • Paper trail over memory. Gate log, goods received note, stock ledger and issue slip each capture one moment in the life of a load. If one is missing, the gap shows up the same day instead of at month-end.
  • Three invoice copies are a cheap audit. Security, store and accounts each hold their own copy, so quantity, rate or vehicle details cannot be changed quietly. Any mismatch becomes visible without the project manager chasing it.
  • Three-way match protects cash. Paying only when the purchase order, goods received note and invoice agree stops payment for material that never arrived or was rejected.
  • Rejection must be quick and signed. A lab next to the store lets a doubtful load be tested at once, and a rejection note signed by the driver stops the argument about what was sent back.
  • Segregated duties. The person who orders, the person who inspects, the person who issues and the person who pays are different people. This is what lets the project manager supervise by checking records, not by standing at the gate.
  • What I would watch. A system only works if it is followed daily. Same-day entries, a weekly record audit and training the store manager on day one matter as much as the formats themselves.

My part, the store layout, showed me that even placement (consumables, non-consumables, equipment and safety gear in marked zones) is a control: a missing item is noticed because its slot is empty.

Conclusion

The procurement, QC, storage and accounts system meets the theme of running with minimum supervision from the project manager.

  • Entry: every vehicle is logged at the gate with vehicle number, driver, time and material.
  • Documents: three invoice copies go to security, the store manager and accounts, and payment follows a three-way match.
  • Quality: QA/QC inspection with the store manager on arrival (cement, steel, aggregate, plywood and safety gear each have their own checklist), with the lab close to the store.
  • Storage and issue: tagged material in marked slots, issued only against a signed slip, with the ledger updated the same day.
  • Supervision: the project manager approves indents and audits the records weekly, and nothing more is needed day to day.

Together these steps turn the store from a person-dependent activity into a repeatable routine that stays sustainable even when staff change.

📐 Problem statement 3

Surveying plan and outsourced work

The Bengaluru survey team charges ₹10,000 plus travel and stay on every visit, so each visit must settle as much work as possible.

Problem statement 3

(Theme: To develop a surveying plan for a particular site and a system to manage in house engineers and outsourced work)

The project execution will start in 5 days. The survey work is outsourced to a Bengaluru-based surveying consultant. Their team equipped with the total station will be traveling to Hubballi for the permanent benchmark location and marking purpose. Using the site layout plan, mark the important benchmark locations throughout the site and mark the RLs when the surveying team arrives. Please keep in mind the surveying team charges Rs.10,000 plus travel and stay expenses every time they come down to the site. Plan your surveying work accordingly to minimize the expenses.

Furthermore, if your site has qualified civil engineers, why did your company outsource the surveying work. Brainstorm the possible reasons.

Minutes of meeting

Tuesday 25/08/2026 · in class

Work distribution for Problem 3.

TaskMember
Benchmark locations marked on the site layoutGayathri
Survey visit schedule and cost (₹10,000 plus travel and stay per visit)Nandish
Reasons for outsourcing the survey workMaitrey
In-house level checks between consultant visitsAnirudh

Solutions

Site visited and interaction with engineer

  • No separate site visit was needed for this problem. The benchmark plan is drawn on my own site layout, using what I saw at the two visits in Problem 1.

Benchmarks

  • One permanent benchmark outside the excavation zone, tied to a known reference
  • Temporary benchmarks near both gates, the labour camp and each block corner
  • Offset pillars and a grid line for each block, protected from vehicles
  • RLs written on every benchmark when the team arrives

Planned visits

  • Visit 1, before excavation: benchmarks, grid, block and basement outlines
  • Visit 2, at basement raft level: verification and column setting-out
  • Visit 3, at plinth: check of axes and levels for the superstructure
  • Everything between visits is done by our engineers with an auto level

Why outsource when we have civil engineers?

  • A total station and its calibration cost far more than a few visits.
  • Third-party survey records give independent proof if a boundary or level dispute arises.
  • Our engineers stay on execution, quality and planning during peak work.
  • Specialist teams are faster and more accurate for control points on a large 8-acre site.

Detailed solution

Survey control plan

  1. Permanent benchmark. The consultant brings a reference level to one permanent benchmark outside the excavation and traffic zone, protected by a concrete block and a fence.
  2. Temporary benchmarks. Four benchmarks near the corners and gates are tied to the permanent one, and each RL is painted on it.
  3. Block set-out. Grid lines and block corners are marked from the total station and fixed on offset pillars.
  4. Verification. Our engineers check levels with an auto level and close every loop back to the benchmark.

Visit planning and cost

VisitPurposeWork done
1: before excavationBenchmarks, grid and block outlinesControl points, RLs, excavation limits
2: basement raft levelVerify depth, set out columnsRaft levels, column positions
3: plinth levelCheck axes for the superstructurePlinth levels, axis check

Three visits cost 3 × ₹10,000 = ₹30,000 plus travel and stay. If the team came eight times, the fees alone would be ₹80,000, so planned visits save ₹50,000 plus five trips of travel and stay.

In-house checks between visits

  • Column verticality with a plumb bob at each lift
  • Floor levels transferred from the benchmark every slab
  • Weekly check of the benchmarks for disturbance

Hold points

  • No raft pour before the consultant verifies levels
  • No column pour before axes and offsets are checked
  • Any benchmark found moved triggers a re-survey call

Reflection

Surveying taught me that the real skill is planning, not measuring. Every visit of the Bengaluru team costs ₹10,000 plus travel and stay, so the question is always what must be settled before they arrive.

  • Timing beats frequency. Three visits tied to milestones (before excavation, basement raft level, plinth level) cost 3 × ₹10,000 = ₹30,000 in fees. Eight ad-hoc visits would cost ₹80,000, so planning saves ₹50,000 plus five trips of travel and stay.
  • One reference for everything. A single protected permanent benchmark outside the excavation and traffic zone means every level on site traces back to the same point. Several unrelated references are how a basement ends up out of level with the superstructure.
  • Protect the control points. A benchmark that is knocked by a truck or buried under spoil is worse than none. The concrete block, fence and painted RLs are cheap compared with re-survey.
  • Outsourcing is a choice, not a verdict on our engineers. It buys calibrated total-station equipment, independent records and more time for our team on execution. Our engineers still close every level loop back to the benchmark between visits.
  • Errors compound. A set-out error found at plinth level means demolition; the same error found at the benchmark stage means repainting an RL. Early checks are the cheapest ones.

I also learnt to mark the benchmark positions on the site layout itself, because survey control has to survive the site changing around it.

Conclusion

The survey plan keeps cost low and levels reliable by combining an outsourced specialist with a disciplined in-house routine.

  • Control: one permanent benchmark plus four temporary benchmarks near the corners and gates, each with its RL painted on it.
  • Visits: three milestone visits, costing ₹30,000 plus travel and stay, instead of repeated unplanned calls.
  • Verification: in-house auto-level checks between visits, with every loop closed on the benchmark.
  • Responsibility: the consultant owns control and set-out, our engineers own day-to-day checks, and each result is recorded.

This division gives accurate set-out at the critical stages without paying for a full-time survey team.

🔩 Problem statement 4

Cutting steel and formwork wastage

History shows 12% steel and 9% plywood wastage. The targets are 5% and 4%, and each stage has a control.

Problem statement 4

(Theme: To reduce wastage of steel and formwork through efficient management)

Your company’s historical data shows the average wastage of steel has been 12% and plywood for formwork wastage has been around 9%. Excavation is in progress for the next 30 days. Use this time to develop a system to have a considerable amount of control over –

  • The calculation of steel required (BBS)
  • The process of ordering the steel (project-wise or block-wise)
  • Storage and releasing it to the fabricators
  • Reconciliation

Please plan and execute your system to bring the wastage of steel down to 5 %.

  • A similar system is to be set up for formwork (reduce wastage by 4 %) –
  • Figure out the different groups of columns and beams based on size.
  • Set up a working procedure to reuse a set of formwork for a minimum of 10 times.

Minutes of meeting

Tuesday 01/09/2026 · in class

Work distribution for Problem 4.

TaskMember
BBS and the ordering approach for steel (block-wise or project-wise)Gayathri
Steel storage, release to fabricators and reconciliationAnirudh
Groups of columns and beams by size for formworkNandish
Formwork reuse procedure for at least 10 usesMaitrey

Solutions

Site visited and interaction with engineer

  • No separate site visit was needed for this problem. The steel and formwork system is planned from the quantities and drawings, with the two visits in Problem 1 as background.

Steel: 12% down to 5%

  • Calculate: bar bending schedule for every block from approved drawings, with cutting lengths planned around 12 m stock bars to reduce offcuts
  • Order: block-wise, a few weeks ahead of each block, so bars are not stored for long and rust
  • Store: racks by diameter with tags, under cover, off the ground
  • Release: to fabricators only against a signed BBS slip
  • Reconcile: weekly, issued weight against used weight plus recorded scrap

Formwork: 9% down to 4%

  • Group columns and beams by size so one set of panels serves many
  • Plan plywood cutting on sheets before cutting, and reuse offcuts for small closures
  • Apply release agent, strip gently and stack flat, aiming for at least 10 reuses per set
  • Carpenters hold a reuse log for each panel set
ControlOwnerFrequency
BBS approvalSite engineerPer block
Steel issue against BBSStore managerDaily
Steel reconciliationProject managerWeekly
Formwork reuse logCarpenter foremanEach pour

Detailed solution

Steel: system from drawing to reconciliation

  1. BBS. Prepare a bar bending schedule for each member from the approved drawings, with bar marks, shapes, diameters, lengths and numbers.
  2. Cutting plan. Combine bar lengths so that 12 m stock bars leave the smallest offcut, and use offcuts for spacers and tie bars.
  3. Ordering. Order block-wise from the BBS total plus a small agreed allowance, so stock arrives close to use.
  4. Storage. Racks by diameter, each lot tagged with its mill certificate, covered and off the ground.
  5. Release. The fabricator receives bars against a signed BBS slip, and finished bars are counted against the slip.
  6. Reconciliation. Run the weekly formula below and investigate any variance above the agreed limit.

Reconciliation formula

Opening stock + received − issued − recorded scrap − closing stock = variance. Weights use standard unit weights for each diameter.

Why 5% matters (assumption: 100 kg of steel per m³)

ItemAt 12% wastageAt 5% wastage
Steel for 12,000 m³1,200 t1,200 t
Wasted steel144 t60 t
Steel saved84 t

Formwork: groups and reuse

Grouping

  • Group columns by section size (for example C1, C2, C3) and beams by width and depth (B1, B2, B3).
  • Build panel sets per group so one set serves many columns.
  • Cut standard panels from full sheets using a cutting plan.

Reuse for 10 cycles

  • Clean and oil panels at every strip.
  • Strip gently, stack flat and cover.
  • Replace damaged edges early and record each use in the reuse log.

Reflection

Past records show 12% steel and 9% plywood wastage. Studying this problem made me see that most of that is decided in the office and the store, before a bar is cut or a panel is made.

  • Planning removes offcuts. A bar bending schedule with cutting lengths planned around 12 m stock bars leaves small, predictable offcuts, and those can be reused as spacers and tie bars.
  • Ordering close to use. Block-wise ordering keeps steel from sitting for months, where it rusts and gets mixed or lost. It also avoids over-ordering for the whole project at the start.
  • Storage is a cost control. Racks by diameter, tags with the mill certificate, cover and a gap from the ground protect both quality and quantity.
  • Issue only against paper. A fabricator who receives bars only against a signed BBS slip is accountable for the weight, and finished bars can be counted against that slip.
  • Reconciliation is what makes it real. Weekly comparison of issued weight with used weight plus recorded scrap turns wastage from a feeling into a number, and variance is investigated while it is still recent.
  • Formwork is about discipline. Grouping columns and beams by size, labelling panels and keeping a reuse log let the same panel serve at least 10 pours. Each careless strip or stack shortens that life.
  • Every control has an owner. Site engineer, store manager, project manager and carpenter foreman each own one check at a fixed frequency, so nothing depends on goodwill.

Wastage is a management problem more than a labour problem, and it falls when people are given a system and are held to it.

Conclusion

The proposed system gives a realistic route from 12% to 5% steel wastage and from 9% to 4% plywood wastage.

  • Steel: BBS for every block, 12 m cutting plan, block-wise ordering, racked storage, issue against signed slips and weekly reconciliation.
  • Formwork: size-wise groups of columns and beams, a reuse procedure for at least 10 uses and a reuse log kept by the carpenter foreman at each pour.
  • Impact: on about 1,200 t of steel (assuming 100 kg per m³ for 12,000 m³), wastage falls from 144 t to 60 t, saving 84 t.
  • Governance: the controls have named owners (site engineer, store manager, project manager, carpenter foreman) and fixed frequencies, from per block to daily and weekly.

The targets are achievable only if the weekly reconciliation is actually run, so that is the control I would protect first.

👷 Problem statement 5

Optimum labour through each stage

12,000 m³ over 468 working days averages about 26 m³ a day, but pours bunch up. Labour follows the work, so peak and slack must both be planned.

Problem statement 5

(Theme: To determine optimum labor force through the various stages of construction)

The concrete required for each Block of this project can be obtained from the Quantity take-off. Based on the given numbers, Figure out the following –

Number of skilled labors (Fabricators, carpenters, masons)

Number of unskilled labors (usually called as the concrete gang)

Keep the following points in mind

  • There will be a peak time during execution where a large number of labor is required and then the slack time when the smaller number will suffice.
  • If you hire less labor, it will impact your productivity
  • If you hire more labor, you won't have enough work to engage them and they will leave.
  • You should have all the prevailing wages in your area and the minimum wage as specified by the government.
  • Your company must sign a contract with the labor supplier, you should know all the legal and technical details of such a contract.

Balancing

  • Too few workers lowers output, too many leaves idle gangs who leave
  • Block-wise sequencing lets the same carpenters and fabricators move from block to block
  • Wages: market rate for the area, never below the government minimum wage
  • Plant crew rates in my cost study: ₹900 skilled, ₹600 unskilled per day

Labour contract

  • Written contract with a licensed labour supplier: scope, rates, duration, notice
  • Registration under BOCW and contract-labour rules where thresholds apply (check the current labour codes)
  • PF, ESI, insurance and safety training in the contract
  • Attendance and payment through bank transfer, with records kept

Detailed solution

Method: concrete to manpower

  1. Quantity per block. Share the 12,000 m³ by floor area (an assumption, since the take-off was not available).
  2. Man-days. Divide each activity quantity by the output norm for one worker or gang per day.
  3. Histogram. Plot workers against time and flatten the peak by sequencing blocks one after another.
  4. Check. Compare the daily wage bill with the productivity gained.

Peak cost and contract

At peak, 120 skilled workers at ₹900 and 100 unskilled workers at ₹600 cost ₹1,08,000 + ₹60,000 = ₹1,68,000 per day. Fewer workers slow the pours, and more leave idle gangs who walk away, so strength rises and falls with the stage.

Labour supplier contract

  • Scope of work, rates and payment dates
  • Licence of the supplier and registration of the workforce
  • PF, ESI, insurance and safety training
  • Minimum wage compliance, working hours and overtime
  • Termination and notice, and penalty for slow progress

Welfare and records

  • Accommodation, water, toilets and first aid as in Problem 1
  • Daily attendance and weekly payment by bank transfer
  • Wage register kept on site for inspection

Reflection

The main thing I learnt is that labour is not a single number. 12,000 m³ over 468 working days averages only about 26 m³ a day, but pours bunch up, and the workforce has to follow the work.

  • Strength follows the stage. My planning figures run from 15 skilled and 40 unskilled for excavation, to 120 skilled and 100 unskilled at the structure peak, to 80 and 50 for masonry and finishing, and 25 and 15 for closing and snagging.
  • Both extremes cost money. Too few workers slow the pours and push the schedule. Too many leave idle gangs, wasted wages and workers who walk away.
  • Sequencing softens the peak. Taking blocks one after another, rather than all seven together, flattens the histogram and avoids paying for a peak for a long time.
  • Quantity first, then manpower. Concrete per block (from 1,424 m³ for Block 5 to 2,034 m³ for Block 7) divided by output norms gives man-days. I shared the volume by floor area only because the take-off was not available, so these figures are indicative and will be replaced by the real take-off.
  • The peak has a real price. 120 skilled at ₹900 and 100 unskilled at ₹600 cost ₹1,68,000 a day, so the case for flattening the peak is a financial one as well as a practical one.
  • A contract protects both sides. Wages at or above the government minimum and a written labour contract protect workers and also protect the company from disputes and compliance problems.

Labour planning is something to revise as the job progresses, comparing the histogram with actual progress every week.

Conclusion

The labour plan matches workforce to stage and keeps productivity high without carrying idle gangs.

  • Strengths: stage-wise skilled and unskilled numbers, peaking at 120 skilled and 100 unskilled during the structure stage.
  • Method: concrete quantity per block, divided by output norms to get man-days, then plotted as a histogram and levelled by sequencing blocks.
  • Cost: about ₹1,68,000 a day at peak, a figure to be weighed against the productivity gained.
  • Compliance: wages above the government minimum and a written contract with each labour contractor.

The numbers are indicative, but the method (quantity to man-days to histogram to wage check) can be reused as soon as the actual take-off is available.

🧪 Problem statement 6

Why 23 of 56 column cubes failed

All 106 footings passed but 23 of 56 columns failed the 28-day test, so the fault lies in something specific to columns or their handling.

Problem statement 6

(Theme: To demonstrate the importance of various tests conducted on site and the ramifications of the failure of material tests)

RCC work is in progress and the work has reached the ground floor level in 3 blocks. Concrete cubes cast during the RCC work of all footings and columns are sent out for testing by a third party testing company. Out of 106 footings cast, all 106 have attained the required strength. But out of 56 columns cast, 23 of them have failed the 28-day compressive strength test. Since your own concrete plant is still being set up, you had used local RMC for this work. The RMC owner has a clause on the contract that states that any failure of strength attainment will be his responsibility and he will bear the expenses to demolish the failed structural component and rebuild it. This clause saved a lot of financial loss to your company. But the RMC contractor still says there was a mistake in the concreting at the site.

Brainstorm to figure out all the possibilities that might have gone wrong. Also, develop a plan that will ensure no concrete cube test will fail in this project hereafter. Also, from the RMC owner’s point of view, what precautions should he take to ensure he does not face such precarious conditions in the future.

Minutes of meeting

Tuesday 15/09/2026 · in class

Work distribution for Problem 6.

TaskMember
Possible causes on the site sideAnirudh
Possible causes on the RMC sideNandish
Plan to prevent cube failures (sampling, handling, curing)Gayathri
Precautions for the RMC ownerMaitrey

Solutions

Site visited and interaction with engineer

  • At Rokhade Castle, concrete came from an RMC supplier or an on-site batching plant, as the work required. This is the same choice I studied in Problem 1.
  • Engineer interaction: see Problem 1.

What may have gone wrong on site

  • Water added to the truck to ease pumping into narrow columns
  • Poor compaction or segregation from a high free-fall of concrete
  • Leaking formwork that washes out cement
  • Cubes cast without proper compaction, left in the sun or knocked in the first 24 hours
  • Weak curing of cubes and of the column itself

What may have gone wrong at the RMC

  • High water-cement ratio or no moisture correction for aggregate
  • Long transit and slump loss
  • Wrong batch weights or uncalibrated scales
  • Wrong admixture dose or cement quality

Plan so no cube fails again

  1. Check delivery challan, time and slump on every truck; reject out-of-range loads and ban water addition.
  2. Sample as per IS 456: 1 sample for 1 to 5 m³, 2 for 6 to 15 m³, 3 for 16 to 30 m³, 4 for 31 to 50 m³, then 1 more per extra 50 m³.
  3. Cast cubes in three layers, tamp, cover, label and store in a shaded area for 24 hours, then cure in water in our site lab.
  4. Use tremie or chutes for columns, vibrate every pour and check formwork for leaks before concreting.
  5. Run 7-day cube checks as an early warning and use a rebound hammer on doubtful columns.

For the RMC owner

  • Calibrate batching scales and test aggregate moisture each day
  • Keep batch records and trial mixes for every grade
  • Control transit time, wash drums and train drivers not to add water
  • Audit customer sites and request cube data on each supply

Detailed solution

Cause analysis

AreaPossible causeHow to check
SiteWater added to the truck, poor compaction, high free fallSlump record, vibration log
SiteLeaking formwork, no curingFormwork inspection, curing register
CubesRough handling, late curing, wrong mouldsCasting and curing log
RMCHigh water-cement ratio, aggregate moisture not correctedBatch records, trial mix
RMCLong transit, slump loss, wrong admixture doseDelivery time, admixture records
TestingMachine error, wrong loading rateCalibration certificates

Five whys (starting point)

  1. Columns failed but footings passed: columns are narrow and harder to place and compact.
  2. Concrete was probably stiff or placed with a long drop, so water was added or compaction was poor.
  3. Truck checks and vibration were not enforced for column pours.
  4. Nobody owned the pour check, so no record caught the problem early.
  5. The fix is a named owner and a mandatory check for every pour.

Corrective and preventive actions

Immediate

  • Test the 23 columns by rebound hammer and cores
  • A structural engineer reviews the results
  • The RMC owner bears the repair as the contract says

Preventive

  • Slump and time check on every truck
  • Sampling as per IS 456 and a cube curing tank on site
  • Shared checklist for the site and the RMC plant

Reflection

All 106 footings passed, but 23 of 56 columns failed the 28-day test. A fault that appears only in columns is a clue, and reading it correctly taught me more than any single test result.

  • Look at the pattern, not just the failure. Footings are wide and easy to place, while columns are narrow and tall. That points to placing, compaction, free fall, water added at the pour, or curing, rather than to the cement or aggregate in general.
  • Responsibility is shared. The RMC plant could have a high water-cement ratio, uncorrected aggregate moisture, long transit or slump loss. The site could have added water to the truck, compacted poorly or cured late. The cubes and the testing machine can also be at fault, so each needs to be checked in turn.
  • Records decide the argument. Slump records, batch records, delivery times, a vibration log, a curing register and calibration certificates are how the truth is found. Without them the dispute becomes one person’s word against another.
  • The RMC clause saved money but not time. The contract made the supplier bear the repair cost, but it could not give back the delay while cores were taken and the structural engineer reviewed the columns.
  • Nobody owned the pour check. My five-whys ends with an organisation problem: no named person was responsible for checking each pour. Testing found the failure, but a daily check would have prevented it.
  • Testing is process control. A 28-day cube result arrives long after the column is cast and loaded. Early signals such as the 7-day check, slump at the truck and rebound hammer on doubtful columns are what let us act in time.

The failed columns show why a test is a control during the work and not a final exam after it.

Conclusion

The 23 failed columns are best explained by a combination of site handling and RMC quality, and the remedy is a set of checks on every pour.

  • Immediate action: test the 23 columns by rebound hammer and cores, have a structural engineer review the results, and enforce the RMC contract for the repair.
  • On site: a slump and time check on every truck, vibration and curing for every pour, formwork checked for leaks, and cubes sampled as per IS 456 and cured in a tank on site.
  • At the RMC plant: calibrated batching scales, daily aggregate moisture checks, trial mixes and batch records for each grade, controlled transit time and no water added at the drum.
  • Shared: one checklist used by both the site and the plant, with a named owner for the pour check.

With truck-by-truck checks, correct cube handling and curing, and an agreed owner for every pour, a repeat of this failure is much less likely.
